terms.comment: Both forms are classical. The feminine sīmia is the commoner (Plautus, Cicero, Pliny) and is used of either sex; the masculine is Phaedrus’s and Martial’s (Lewis & Short), and the one this lexicon leads with.

evidence: Plaut. Mil. 2.2.7; Cic. Div. 1.76; Plin. NH 8.215 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The commoner classical form (Plautus, Cicero, Pliny), used of either sex; sīmius is Phaedrus’s and Martial’s (Lewis & Short).

phrases.english: You monkey! (as a term of abuse)

phrases.latin: Sīmius mihi petasum surripuit et in arborem aufūgit!
phrases.english: A monkey stole my hat and ran off up a tree!

phrases.latin: Cavē: sīmiī hīc quicquid vident surripiunt.
phrases.english: Watch out: the monkeys here steal anything they see.
Don’t feed the monkeys; they bite.

phrases.latin: Nē quid sīmiīs dederīs; audāciōrēs enim fīunt.
phrases.english: Don’t give the monkeys anything: it makes them bolder.

sources: Lewis & Short: simius / simia
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 141, 143, 272, 347.
